extracted.intended_audience: general public; people seeking an encyclopedic overview of Comic Relief / Red Nose Day (donors, journalists, researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article describing the British charity Comic Relief (founding, Red Nose Day telethon, fundraising methods, merchandise, controversies, and history). Useful for readers wanting a factual summary of the organisation and its practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission / Grant‑making principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The charity says its aim is to "bring about positive and lasting change in the lives of poor and disadvantaged people, which we believe requires investing in work that addresses people's immediate needs as well as tackling the root causes of poverty and injustice".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statement functions as Comic Relief's overarching grant‑making standard: fund both immediate relief and projects tackling root causes. The article references a "Vision & Principles for UK grant-making" on Comic Relief's site (archived).

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Pound Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the fundamental principles behind working at Comic Relief is the "Golden Pound Principle" where every donated pound (£) is spent on charitable projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operating costs (staff salaries, production etc.) are covered by corporate sponsors or interest earned on money waiting to be distributed. The BBC, BT Group, TK Maxx and British Airways are cited as main supporters fulfilling operational support roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundraising model / channel diversification
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundraising uses multiple channels: the Red Nose Day telethon, Sport Relief (historically), countrywide sponsored events, merchandise (notably red noses), charity singles, celebrity challenges and televised programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents examples (telethons, merchandise, charity singles, sponsored challenges and PR events) and notes that merchandise and sponsored events contribute significant funds alongside on‑the‑night donations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television programming format for Red Nose Day
rubrics_metrics.description: Telethon programming begins in the afternoon (CBBC segments), with a main live evening show on BBC One (and breaks on BBC Two for News). The live show features parodies, specially filmed comedy versions of shows, musical performances and celebrity hosting teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common themes: parodies of popular shows/films, specially filmed comedy sketches, and each hour overseen by different celebrity teams who work for free; production facilities are donated by the BBC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity participation and cost model
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrities present material and appear on the telethon, and do the work free; crew, studio space and production facilities are typically donated by the BBC; corporate partners provide telephony, merchandising support and sponsorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model is described as part of how Comic Relief minimises fundraising overheads and ensures most donated money goes to projects (linked to the Golden Pound Principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Red Nose design / annual re‑design policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The design of the red nose has been changed each year in part "to stop people from re-using previous years designs, and having to buy the latest version".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article lists many yearly designs and notes strategies such as multiple designs, mystery bags, rare/ultra‑rare variants and packaging choices used to drive repeat purchases and collectibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of limited/rare variants as fundraising tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic Relief has used 'rare' and 'ultra-rare' noses, 'golden' noses and hidden golden versions to incentivise purchases and engagement (e.g., mystery bags with hidden golden versions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 2015's nine‑design mystery bags with hidden golden versions, and later years' rare/ultra‑rare noses; these are explicitly tied to fundraising totals and marketing campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchandise sustainability / material policy
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to environmental concerns, Comic Relief introduced plant‑based, plastic‑free red noses (2021), used bagasse (sugarcane waste), wood pulp, biofoam and other materials in subsequent years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents material choices by year (e.g., bagasse in 2021 and 2022, 70% bagasse/30% wood pulp in 2024, biofoam in 2025) and frames these as a sustainability/ethical sourcing response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchandise ethical sourcing (Fairtrade etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic Relief have sold Fairtrade Cotton Socks and other ethically‑sourced merchandise (noted mainly for Sport Relief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates a criterion to align merchandise with ethical trade/sourcing where practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health and safety / regulatory compliance for merchandise
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchandise and promotional items have to meet safety standards — e.g., a large inflatable nose's material was classed as a fire hazard and banned from a show; car nose designs were changed (magnetic design introduced and later grill‑attachable designs returned) owing to safety concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records past bans and design changes prompted by safety/regulatory issues; implies merchandise must comply with health & safety and broadcasting regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital and interactive engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic Relief has used digital/interactive features to engage donors: augmented reality noses, a 'Red Nose' app (AR), online games, and social media campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include AR webcams converting a user's head into a giant red nose, the 'Red Nose' app, online games tied to campaigns and use of social media to promote donations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and reporting of fundraising outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic Relief publicly reports amounts raised for each Red Nose Day and publishes totals (including inflation‑adjusted figures in the article's tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides yearly on‑the‑night and total fundraising figures, cites BARB for viewing figures and documents totals raised across years, indicating an expectation of open reporting of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of exploitative imagery and 'white saviour' portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: Following criticism (e.g., 'white saviour' rows and accusations of 'poverty porn'), Comic Relief committed to changes such as cutting back on celebrity appeals, dropping certain imagery and 'stop sending celebrities to Africa' and to 'stop using images of starving children in Africa for Red Nose Day'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites public criticism and subsequent policy shifts (e.g., pledges to ditch white saviour stereotype appeals), which function as standards for ethical representation in fundraising communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment and reputational risk sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic Relief faced criticism when money was reported as invested in arms and tobacco shares, highlighting that investment choices can be a source of reputational risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the article reports the criticism rather than an explicit investment policy, it implies an evaluative criterion that charitable organisations should avoid investments in sectors (e.g., arms, tobacco) that contradict their mission and public expectations.
